issues: The major plank of the appellants' submissions is that the repeal of Act of 1947 is the reason why the entire prosecution is vitiated.
petitioner_arguments: The alleged crime took place between 9/7/1988 and 14/07/1988 and FIR was lodged in respect of the same on 19/02/1990 alleging offences under the Act of 1947. Counsel submitted that FIR could not have been lodged for the offences punishable under the Act of 1947, which stood repealed by the New Act. It was urged that in fact, by reason of repeal, proceedings under the Act of 1947 stand obliterated. In this connection, our attention was drawn to S. 30 of the New Act. Sub-s. 1 of S. 2 thereof provides for repeal and saving. It states that the Act of 1947 stands repealed. It was pointed out that Sub-s. 2 of S. 30 of the New Act states that notwithstanding such repeal, but without prejudice to the application of S. 6 of the General Clauses Act, anything done or any action taken or purported to have been done or taken under or in pursuance of the Acts so repealed shall, in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of the New Act be deemed to have been done or taken under or in pursuance of the corresponding provisions of the New Act. Counsel submitted that since no action was taken under the Act of 1947, there was no question of coming to a conclusion that any action taken could be deemed to have been taken under the provisions of the New Act. Since no action was taken under the Act of 1947, there was no question of saving it. Counsel also drew our attention to S. 6 of the GC Act which speaks about the effect of repeal. Counsel submitted that the instant case is not covered by any of the sub-clauses of S. 6 of the GC Act so as to come to a conclusion that any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced or any penalty or punishment may be imposed as if the repealing Act had not been passed.
respondent_arguments: Mr. Chandhiok, learned Additional Solicitor General, for the C.B.I. supported the impugned judgment.
court_reasoning: We are unable to accept the submissions of learned counsel for the appellants. It is true that according to the prosecution, the alleged offence took place between 9/7/1988 and 14/07/1988. The New Act came into force on 9/9/1988. The FIR was registered against the appellants, inter alia, for offences punishable under the Act of 1947. Charges were framed against the appellants, inter alia, under the provisions of the Act of 1947 and the appellants were tried and convicted as aforesaid. Since the repeal of Act of 1947 is the major plank of the appellants' submissions, it is necessary to quote S. 30 of the New Act which repealed the Act of 1947. It reads thus: '30. Repeal and saving:- (1) The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (2 of 1947) and the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 (46 of 1952) are hereby repealed. (2) Notwithstanding such repeal, but without prejudice to the application of s. 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897), anything done or any action taken or purported to have been done or taken under or in pursuance of the Acts so repealed shall, in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be deemed to have been done or taken under or in pursuance of the corresponding provision of this Act.' Sub-s. 1 of S. 30 makes it clear that the Act of 1947 has been repealed. Sub-s. 2 of S. 30 of the New Act says that anything done or any action taken or purported to have been done or taken under or in pursuance of the repealed Acts in so far as it is not inconsistent with the New Act, shall be deemed to have been done or taken in pursuance of the New Act. Thus, a deeming fiction is introduced so far as action taken under the repealed Act is concerned.
holding: We are unable to accept the submissions of learned counsel for the appellants. The appeal is dismissed.
